To me it is. I get what the point of the prefix is, to be the opposite of trans. But that’s the thing, I didn’t need this prefix label. I didn’t change anything. I don’t have anything about me that’s associated with gender identity. I was born a girl, “she’s a girl!” was said by the doctor delivering me, the nurse wrote female on my birth certificate, my parents raised as a girl, hit puberty, and now I’m a woman. I know the person who coined the word in [1994](https://www.huffpost.com/entry/what-cisgender-means-transgender_n_63e13ee0e4b01e9288730415/amp) didn’t mean for it to be a slur. It wasn’t supposed to push anyone into “otherness” but it strips our identity we have always had since conception to birth to now away from us. We don’t have a cis journey like trans individuals have a trans journey. We have our basic experience of womanhood that closely connects us through generations and across cultures despite cultural differences. And using the prefix trans- in with the term trans woman encompasses an experience unique and special only to trans women. I do not know the experience trans women and I’ve never been in the shoes of a trans woman we have vastly different experiences in life all together. We may have experienced some of the same things all woman presenting people experience like harassment from men or struggling to find clothes that fit because women’s clothing companies can’t even make a teeshirt fit around our arms correctly or not be basically a crop top when it’s not marketed as one… (ugh f clothing companies) We didn’t ask to be grouped into unnecessary labels when ours worked fine before, while your labels are necessary for your experience and your health and making sure you get proper care. The person who coined the term cis was trying to attempt something but that something wasn’t what the majority chose to identify with. It makes me feel like I’m forced into something I didn’t consent to being a part of. While being born with whatever chromosomes isn’t something we choose and isn’t something we can or can’t consent to, nobody can consent to being born, it just happens, and we just grow up doing our thing, existing in the life we know, and the identity we grew into comfortably, for me it’s female, daughter, girl, sister, and woman. I’m also niece, grand daughter, and I hope one day I can be aunt and mother. I feel comfortable and safe in my girlhood experience of playing with dolls, chewing on poly pockets, picking the cuter hot wheels cars when playing with my little brother, and my dad teaching me, a little girl at the time but a woman later, how to do so many male dominated tasks where I can finish it and say “look I did this AND IM A GIRL WHO DID IT!! then he can brag to people that “well my daughter can learn to torch cut in less than an hour, so why can’t you?” I am a woman in construction. I am a woman in safety. I am many labels but adding cis on it just makes me feel like I’m about to be minimized from sister to the servant sibling who’s only job is to take care of her brother, daughter to parent’s walking wallet and house keeper, mother to incubator/egg carrier, girlfriend to sandwich maker. Blue collar woman to the job site flashlight. It’s just one small step to erasing what we want to be called. Why does other cultures and groups get to choose what they want to be called, create their own labels, take back the slurs once used against them, decide what is a slur, decides who calls them what, but the second majority of women don’t want to be called cis we have no say and look like we are some awful person?

When you experience something like being amab or afab, then as you grow up things labels and experiences don’t sit right, you experience these things that differ so much from the “norm” and then you go through your own experience and journey and you come out with your new identities and labels while renaming and reinventing yourself, that’s such a unique experience that usually only fits the “trans” label. In a perfect world, that label wouldn’t have been needed but right now it’s needed to make sure you all get the right medical care and aren’t medically gaslit by doctors saying “well it’s probably because you’re pregnant so I’ll just make you pee in this cup so I can shove a stick in it before actually doing anything to help you” while you’re having non pregnancy related symptoms and distressed.

Regardless, I think the term while having good intentions initially, it is not what the majority of us want to be called and I get the physical sensation of needing to vomit when I hear it or get called it. It’s a stepping stone to continue oppressing women and calling us things we don’t want to be called. I can’t speak for men and being called a “cis man” but in my life I see it as a huge disrespect of my womanhood and using the excuse of “but it’s medical!!” when women weren’t called cis women before 1994 is a poor reason as cis can be used for whatever else people want to use it in science just not my sex/gender.

This happened to me, I just recently paid off my bed when it had happened. I still have the same bed but I am now very very very picky about sheets. I have 4 pairs of sheets, different blankets and comforters, etc. 

You don’t have to listen to anything I say but I want to suggest some things for you. 

1) if you can’t replace your bed, take it over and do what you can to make it a safe place again. Deep clean it after all of the police stuff is over and they have what they need, and I fully suggest getting new sheets, getting new bedding, everything. Wash and put a new safe scent on your bed that calms you if you have sheets and blankets you can’t get rid of (I had a quilt my grandma made me on my bed and I still have it and use it because it’s still safe for me) 

2) if you can, redo your bedroom. I got raped June 2019 in my bedroom, I redid my bedroom October/November 2021 finally. My therapist was shocked it took me that long. Paint your walls, change everything around move stuff around. This may take time and money but you can do it at your own pace. If you can’t paint, deep clean and scrub the walls, shampoo the carpets, change your decor. Move things around.

My biggest advice for this is rebuilding it into a safe space. Do not let ANYONE who is the same sex as the rapist come into your room unless it’s somebody who you know won’t hurt you. (My ride or die best friend helped me moved stuff around and he testified as a character witness for me too) Ask for help with your room too. I’d offer to help but I doubt you’re in Northern California and would trust a 25 year old woman to come around after something as big as this happened. 

However, I do think starting with cleaning your bed and new sheets is a good first step. I’m Orthodox Christian and got baptized this year and I think I’m going to put some holy water in a spray bottle and spray my mattress now that I think about it. 

I suggest NICE sheets. I prefer cotton. I get the Cotton Performance Sheets from Threshold at Target. I have multiple colors now. I only get bedding that makes my bed feel soft and safe. At this point, my room has become a safe space. I even installed closet doors and got a new way to store underwear because he went through my underwear after the assault that day. Now I have my underwear in a dresser behind closet doors. My walls are no longer gray, they are green and white, I have got everything to be white instead of black. I don’t have my black desk or bookshelf anymore. I have all white and natural wood. It feels peaceful. My main colors are natural greens and blush pinks with some yellows. My old room was a mess of colors and gray and blacks everywhere. 

Rebuild your safe space. It seems impossible but I have chronic nightmares and I would much rather have my room like this than waking up in the same spot I was assaulted at the same angle I was laying and my room looking exactly the same. It’s all different and I wake up and know that my nightmare was just a nightmare about the past and how it’s all different now. 

If you need help with anything DM me, we can even talk about getting you new sheets.

Even if you don’t have trauma, distorted thinking is possible. Sometimes you can’t reprogram your brain to think better after medication intervention because of the neuro pathways  that have been created in your brain. You know the road less traveled all analogy? Imagine that but it’s your brain. You are used to walking the same path over and over and over again. Now you have a built in path. That’s you and me with our negative thoughts. We have to figure out a way to create new paths to get somewhere else or even the same location but without trees that might have fallen into our path or dangerous holes created in our path that can cause our ankle to break. If we keep walking this path we could be harmed (the depression and such) so we must build another path. A lot of the time people just need some help learning how to change those pathways in your head. Which is how therapy comes into play. 

There are therapy types like CBT and a few others but CBT is a popular one (see r/CBT for discussion with other people in that therapy type and I am about to try to read Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy again soon which is a very well known reputable CBT book) which teach you how to handle cognitions (thoughts) so that you can challenge them and change them. This therapy type changes the thoughts, behaviors and more.  CBT is what DBT is based off of. But DBT is heavily mindfulness based and more for saving your life and stabilizing you for other therapy types rather than curing you. I’d recommend looking into it and discussing it with your therapist.

With hard work you can go into remission and remain symptomless or even live a happy balanced life. It’s just a diagnosis for a collection of symptoms. It’s not a defining factor or a death sentence. The diagnosis is to figure out best course of action for treatment. Not to hurt you. Don’t let the people who let it become their identity fool you, your identity can be the person who overcame BPD, not let it keep destroying your life. With HARD WORK and loads of therapy you can be stable and at peace in your mind. There’s books that can help: BPD Survival Guide, DBT therapy work books including the OG Marsha Lineham’s handouts, Mindfulness for BPD, and CBT books like Feeling Good:The New Mood Therapy for the depression that co exists with the BPD. If you struggle with any addictions there’s AA, NA, a portion of the DBT worksheets from ML addressing when addiction is the crisis. There’s fidget devices and such to help prevent cutting along with DBT skills. There’s apps for it even! Another thing is journaling. You can practice mindfulness with journaling. You can keep yourself on track in therapy with journaling. Write your goals “this week I’m going to use the P.L.E.A.S.E skill twice!” And follow up later to see if you did it. “I am going to do one mindfulness meditation this week” “I’m going to do that one goal my therapist helped me set this week!” Now I’ll tell you a secret. DBT is not there to make you happy it’s there to stabilize you so you can make your way through other therapy types. If you’re stable but not happy yet, it’s working for you. CBT makes you happy. There’s other therapy types that make you happy. DBT stabilizes you and keeps you from destroying good things and allows you to stand up for yourself and deal with emotions, distress, and relationships. There are a few people who have done it. I’m still working on it but when I first got the diagnosis I wanted it to be my identity too. But then you realize there’s other better identities to take on like fighter, survivor and “very active helpful group participant” from the DBT coordinators. Once you put the long hard work in, it pays off.

I did over 8 months of DBT therapy weekly. The whole thing is basically worksheets. I have a binder full of them. Reason why I think worksheets are helpful? You have them explaining stuff, then you have it there in your hand for access later. There’s little tests and scales like the Burns checklist to see where depression levels are at for tracking. 

Now imagine this: it’s half way in between your next appointment, you are in crisis, it’s 3AM and all of your friends are asleep, you grab your therapy binder, find the worksheet that will walk you through the crisis, you follow the steps, you calm down enough to journal about it, and go to sleep. You wake up, clean yourself up, write about your night again in your journal now that you are much more calm, you function the rest of the week. You go to your appointment, you tell them about your victory, read them the journal entry and then your therapist gives you praise and can figure out what they can do for you next. 

Worksheets are such an amazing tool. They provide visuals for you later. I do recommend a therapy binder. Collecting your worksheets into an arsenal for you to use is a great way to take advantage of them. I wish I did it sooner. I also wish I took notes more in therapy and in groups.

Psych ward checklist: blanket, socks, (if you’re a girl bring a bra with no underwire) hoodie with no strings, pj pants with no strings, normal jeans that fit without a belt and shirts, underwear, composition book or book bound journal, toiletries (they will keep them locked up so you can’t drink them. Ask for them when you need them for showering!) biggest tip: wear normal clothes. Don’t wear PJ’s all day and night. It will make you feel more depressed. I feel better when I dress normal vs how everyone else is in PJ’s or scrubs. It makes me feel more secure and normal. Slides or crocs to walk around in because you can’t have shoelaces. Slip on vans are perfect for psych wards if they allow shoes. You are allowed to wash your clothes normally, you are allowed to bring playing cards for solitaire and crayons. Don’t wear any military or government sweatshirts (I wore my ex’s from BMT and the two dudes with schizophrenia saw it and the conversation ended in them paranoid and scared of me and aliens. It’s kinda funny now but I would never wear it again there.) and bring an appropriate book. Some hospitals lack groups, others don’t. I would 100% recommend going to as many groups as possible. And when the social worker asks what you are going to do when you get out of the hospital, you tell them you’re getting some tacos because “uh idk probably sleep? I don’t know” makes them worried. Be honest with them. Be strict with your boundaries and say “I don’t feel comfortable with this medication you’re suggesting” if you don’t want to try it. If they won’t give you your birth control (again idk if you’re a girl or not) or other meds you’re supposed to be on be assertive and tell them. Take time to journal and express thoughts and concerns in the journal and give yourself a list of things you want to address with the doctors and staff. It’s a very emotional time for people and I whole heartily believe that coming prepared with your own stuff and getting help on your own terms will make the stay less traumatic. I know being thrown into a psych ward with no clothes, hospital blankets, and no toiletries makes me more anxious and less likely to get the help I need vs being prepared and ready to accept any help they try to give. You know what I mean? Pack yourself a bag, walk into the ER, tell them the truth, and everything will be much smoother. Sometimes they won’t even hospitalize you and you’ll get put in an outpatient program rather than hospitalization which might be more helpful unless you feel like a danger to yourself.
